short: Investment by specialist funds that buy big stakes in companies not listed on a stock exchange, improve them over years, then sell at a profit.
kid: Some grown-ups put their coins together to buy a whole toy shop. They fix it up and make it nicer, then later sell it to someone else for more coins than they paid.
detail: Private equity (PE) is money invested in companies outside the public stock market. A PE firm raises a fund from investors such as pension funds, insurers, endowments and family offices (the limited partners), while its own team (the general partner) picks and manages the deals. Common strategies are buyouts of mature companies, often using borrowed money (leveraged buyouts), growth investments in expanding firms, and taking listed companies private. A fund usually runs about ten years: it invests in the first few, then sells each holding through an IPO, a sale to a company or a sale to another fund. Managers typically earn a yearly management fee plus a share of profits called carried interest. In India, PE funds register with SEBI as alternative investment funds. Common confusions: venture capital is the part of PE that backs young startups, and 'PE' in market news can also mean the price-to-earnings ratio.
example: Say a PE fund buys 60% of XYZ Foods Pvt Ltd for ₹600 crore, valuing the whole company at ₹1,000 crore. Five years later the company is worth ₹2,500 crore, so the fund sells its 60% stake for ₹1,500 crore, or 2.5 times the money it put in.
formula: Multiple on invested capital (MOIC) = Total value received / Total amount invested

short: Money that specialist investors put into young, fast-growing startups in exchange for part-ownership, accepting high risk for the chance of very large gains.
kid: A new lemonade stand needs coins to buy its first cups. A helper gives the coins and gets a small piece of the stand, hoping it grows into a big juice shop one day.
detail: Venture capital (VC) is a form of private equity that funds young, high-growth companies, usually before they make a profit. A VC firm raises a fund from limited partners and invests in a portfolio of startups across rounds such as seed, Series A and later, typically taking minority stakes through preference shares with negotiated rights. Most startups fail or return little, so VC follows a power law: one or two big winners must pay for the losses across the whole fund. VCs also help through board seats, hiring support and introductions. Returns arrive only at exit, through an acquisition or an IPO. In India, VC funds register with SEBI as alternative investment funds, usually Category I or II. A common confusion: a VC is not a lender. It gets no fixed repayment and makes money only if the company's shares become valuable.
example: Say a VC fund invests $1 million each in 20 startups, $20 million in total. If 15 fail, 4 return $2 million each and 1 returns $40 million, the fund gets back $48 million, or 2.4 times its money, almost all of it from one winner.

short: A young company built to grow very fast by solving a problem in a new way, usually funded by outside investors before it earns profits.
kid: A startup is a brand-new little shop with a big idea. It starts tiny and hopes to grow very big, very fast.
detail: A startup is a newly founded company designed to grow quickly, typically by using technology or a new business model to reach a large market. What separates it from an ordinary small business is ambition and scalability: a neighbourhood bakery aims for steady profit, while a startup aims to multiply its revenue many times over, often running losses for years along the way. Startups usually raise money in stages from angel investors and venture capital funds, giving up part of their ownership each time. In India, the government's Startup India scheme, run by DPIIT, recognises eligible young companies and offers certain tax and compliance benefits; the eligibility conditions, such as limits on age and turnover, are set by notification and have changed over time. A common confusion: being new does not make a company a startup in the investor sense; the high-growth, investor-funded model does.
example: Say two friends launch an app-based tiffin service, ABC Meals, with ₹10 lakh of savings. A year later an angel investor puts in ₹50 lakh for 10% of the company, valuing it at ₹5 crore after the investment, even though it is still making losses.

short: An organisation that helps very new startups get going by giving them workspace, mentoring and shared services, usually over a longer, flexible period.
kid: An incubator is like a warm nest where baby birds stay safe until they can fly. Little new businesses stay there and get help until they are strong enough on their own.
detail: An incubator supports startups at the idea or very early stage, often before there is a finished product. It typically provides low-cost workspace, mentors, legal and accounting help, lab or tech facilities and links to investors. Programmes are usually open-ended, lasting from several months to a couple of years, and many incubators are run by universities, governments or large companies rather than by investors. Some take a small equity stake or charge a fee; others are grant-funded. In India, many incubators sit inside academic institutions such as the IITs and IIMs, and schemes such as the Atal Innovation Mission and the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme route support through them. A common confusion: an incubator nurtures an idea at its own pace, while an accelerator runs a short, fixed-length programme for startups that already have a product, usually in exchange for equity.
example: Say a student team joins a campus incubator that gives it desk space and mentoring for 18 months in return for 2% of the company. If the company is later valued at ₹20 crore and the incubator still owns 2%, its stake is worth ₹40 lakh on paper.

short: A short, fixed-length programme that gives young startups a small investment, intense mentoring and investor introductions, usually in exchange for a slice of ownership.
kid: Think of a summer camp for new little shops. For a few months, coaches help them get better quickly, and at the end they show off to grown-ups who might help them grow.
detail: An accelerator takes in a batch, or cohort, of startups that usually already have a product or early customers, and runs an intensive programme lasting roughly three to six months. Startups get a small cheque, structured mentoring, workshops and access to a network of founders and investors, and the programme ends with a demo day where they pitch to investors. In return the accelerator usually takes equity, often somewhere around 5% to 10%. Y Combinator in the US, founded in 2005, is the best-known example; its standard terms have changed over the years, so check the current deal rather than quoting a fixed one. India has accelerators run by VC firms, corporates and government bodies. A common confusion: accelerators speed up startups that already exist and take equity, while incubators nurture earlier ideas over a longer, looser period.
example: Say an accelerator invests $150,000 in a startup for 7% of the company. That implies a post-money valuation of $150,000 / 0.07, or about $2.14 million.

short: A wealthy individual who invests their own money in very young startups, often before any professional fund will, in return for part-ownership.
kid: An angel is a kind grown-up who gives a child coins to start a lemonade stand. In return, they get a small part of whatever the stand earns later.
detail: An angel investor is an individual, often a successful entrepreneur or senior professional, who backs startups at the pre-seed or seed stage with personal money. Cheques are smaller than a VC fund's, and angels typically invest through equity, convertible notes or SAFE-style instruments. Besides money, angels often bring advice, credibility and contacts that help founders raise their next round. Because most very young startups fail, angels usually spread small amounts across many companies. Many invest together through angel networks such as Indian Angel Network to share deal screening and pool cheques, and SEBI rules also allow angel funds as a type of registered alternative investment fund. A common confusion: angels invest their own money, while venture capitalists invest money raised from other people in a fund, which changes their incentives and how fast they decide.
example: Say an angel puts ₹25 lakh into ABC Robotics at a ₹2.5 crore post-money valuation, getting 10% of the company. If later rounds dilute that stake to 5% and the company is sold for ₹100 crore, the angel receives ₹5 crore, 20 times the original cheque.

short: The very first money a startup raises, often from its founders, family, friends or angels, to turn an idea into a first product.
kid: Before you can open a lemonade stand, Mum and Grandpa give you a few coins for lemons and a jug. That first little help to get started is what this is.
detail: Pre-seed funding is the earliest outside money a startup takes, usually when it has an idea, a founding team and perhaps a prototype but little or no revenue. Sources include the founders' own savings, friends and family, angel investors, incubators and a growing number of specialist pre-seed funds. Amounts are small and are often raised through convertible notes or SAFEs rather than priced shares, because putting a precise value on an idea is hard. The money pays for building a first basic version of the product, testing whether customers want it and gathering evidence for a seed round. The line between pre-seed and seed is blurry and has shifted as round sizes have grown. A common confusion: friends and family money is still an investment with legal terms, so it should be properly documented, since loose early promises can complicate the cap table later.
example: Say the founders of ABC Health raise ₹40 lakh from family and one angel and give up 8% of the company. That implies a post-money valuation of ₹40 lakh / 0.08 = ₹5 crore.

short: An early round of outside investment that helps a startup with a first product find customers and prove its business can work.
kid: You plant a tiny seed and give it water so it can grow into a plant. This money is the water that helps a tiny new business start growing.
detail: Seed funding is usually the first formal round a startup raises from professional investors, after or instead of a pre-seed round. By this stage the company often has a product and early users, and the money pays for hiring, product development and finding product-market fit, the point where customers clearly want what is being sold. Seed investors include angels, angel networks, accelerators and seed-focused VC funds. Rounds may be priced, where investors buy shares at an agreed valuation, or use convertible instruments such as SAFEs and convertible notes. Founders often sell somewhere around 10% to 25% of the company in a seed round, though this varies widely. A common confusion: the label tracks stage, not size; in some boom years seed rounds in India and abroad grew so large that they looked like earlier Series A rounds.
example: Say XYZ Pay raises a seed round of ₹6 crore at a pre-money valuation of ₹24 crore. The post-money valuation is ₹30 crore, so the seed investors own ₹6 crore / ₹30 crore = 20% of the company.
formula: Investor ownership = Amount invested / Post-money valuation

short: A startup's first big venture capital round after seed money, used to scale a proven product; later rounds are Series B, C and so on.
kid: When a little lemonade stand shows that lots of people love its lemonade, grown-ups give it a much bigger bag of coins to open more stands. Each new, bigger bag gets the next letter: A, then B, then C.
detail: Series A is usually the first large priced equity round led by a venture capital fund, raised once a startup has shown product-market fit through traction such as revenue growth, user numbers or customer retention. Investors typically receive preference shares carrying rights set out in a term sheet, such as a liquidation preference, anti-dilution protection and often a board seat. Each later round takes the next letter: Series B usually funds expansion, Series C and D fund scaling, new markets or acquisitions, and late-stage rounds may bring in PE funds, crossover funds and sovereign wealth funds before an IPO. Each round normally comes at a higher valuation and dilutes existing holders. A common confusion: the letter shows order and maturity, not a fixed amount; one company's Series A can be larger than another's Series C.
example: Say ABC Logistics raises a $10 million Series A at a $40 million pre-money valuation, so the post-money valuation is $50 million and the new investors own 20%. Two years later it raises a $30 million Series B at a $120 million pre-money valuation; the Series B investors get $30 million / $150 million = 20%, and every earlier holder's stake shrinks by one-fifth.

short: A smaller, temporary round of money that keeps a startup running until its next big funding round or another planned event, such as a sale.
kid: When you are halfway across a stream, a friend puts down a plank so you can reach the other side. This money is that plank, helping a business get to its next big step.
detail: A bridge round is interim financing that covers the gap between two priced rounds, or between a round and an exit. It is usually raised from existing investors, often through convertible notes or SAFEs so that no new valuation has to be set, and the money converts into shares at the next priced round, often at a discount or under a valuation cap. An extension round is similar: extra money added to a round that has already closed, such as a 'Series A extension'. A bridge can be positive, giving a growing company time to hit milestones and win a better valuation, or a warning sign, when a company cannot raise a full round and insiders are keeping it alive. A common confusion: a startup bridge round usually turns into equity, unlike a bridge loan in corporate finance, which is short-term debt repaid from a planned refinancing or sale.
example: Say ABC Foods has 4 months of cash left and expects to raise its Series B in 9 months. Its existing investors put in ₹15 crore as convertible notes with a 20% discount; if Series B shares are priced at ₹500, the bridge investors convert at ₹400 per share and receive 3,75,000 shares.

short: A short slide presentation that founders use to explain their business, market, team and funding needs to possible investors.
kid: It is a little picture book you show to grown-ups to explain your lemonade stand idea and why they should help. Each page tells one part of the story.
detail: A pitch deck is the slide presentation, usually 10 to 20 slides, that a startup uses to raise money. It typically covers the problem, the solution, market size, business model, traction (revenue, users or growth so far), competition, the team, financial projections and the ask: how much money is being raised and what it will be spent on. Investors often see the deck before meeting the founders, so it must make the case quickly and clearly. A short teaser version may be emailed, while a fuller one is presented in meetings. The deck only starts the conversation; detailed checks, called due diligence, and the term sheet come later. A common confusion: a pitch deck is not a business plan or a financial model. It tells the story in brief, and investors then test its claims against data, customer calls and the numbers behind the projections.
example: Say a startup's deck asks for ₹8 crore and plans to spend 50% on product and engineering, 30% on sales and marketing and 20% on operations staff. That is ₹4 crore, ₹2.4 crore and ₹1.6 crore respectively.

short: A short, mostly non-binding document listing the main terms of a proposed investment, such as amount, valuation and investor rights, before the final legal contracts.
kid: Before friends swap toys, they write a little note saying who gets what and what the rules are. Later they make it official, but the note shows they agree on the big things.
detail: A term sheet summarises the main terms an investor proposes: the amount, the pre-money valuation, the type of security (usually preference shares in venture deals), liquidation preference, anti-dilution protection, board seats, voting and veto rights, the employee option pool, founder vesting, and share transfer rights such as ROFR, tag-along and drag-along. Most clauses are non-binding, but a few, such as confidentiality, exclusivity (a 'no-shop' period) and governing law, usually are binding. After signing, the investor carries out due diligence and lawyers turn the term sheet into final documents; in India these are typically a share subscription agreement and a shareholders' agreement, with key rights also written into the company's articles of association. A common confusion: a signed term sheet is not money in the bank. Deals can still fall apart during diligence, so it should not be treated as a closed round.
example: Say a term sheet offers ₹20 crore at an ₹80 crore pre-money valuation with a 1x non-participating liquidation preference. The post-money valuation would be ₹100 crore, so the investor would own ₹20 crore / ₹100 crore = 20% of the company.

short: What a company is agreed to be worth just before new investors put their money in.
kid: Before a friend adds new toys to your toy box, you both agree how much the box is already worth. That agreed amount is the before number.
detail: Pre-money valuation is the value placed on a company's equity immediately before a funding round; adding the new money gives the post-money valuation. Founders and investors negotiate it, and it directly sets how much of the company the new investor gets: for a fixed investment, a higher pre-money valuation means a smaller stake for the investor and less dilution for founders. The round's share price is usually the pre-money valuation divided by the fully diluted shares before the round, which typically includes the employee option pool. That detail matters: if the term sheet requires the option pool to be created or enlarged before the round, the cost falls on existing shareholders, so the effective pre-money valuation is lower than the headline figure. A common confusion: news reports often quote a startup's valuation without saying whether it is pre-money or post-money, and the two differ by the size of the round.
example: Say an investor puts ₹10 crore into ABC Tech at a pre-money valuation of ₹40 crore. The post-money valuation is ₹50 crore, so the investor owns 20%. If 40 lakh shares existed before the round, the price is ₹40 crore / 40 lakh = ₹100 per share, and the investor receives 10 lakh new shares.
formula: Pre-money valuation = Post-money valuation - New investment; Price per share = Pre-money valuation / Fully diluted shares before the round

short: What a company is worth right after a new investment, equal to its value just before the round plus the new money raised.
kid: Your toy box was worth ten sweets, and a friend adds toys worth five more sweets. Now the whole box is worth fifteen sweets, and that after number is what this means.
detail: Post-money valuation is the value of a company's equity immediately after a funding round closes. It equals the pre-money valuation plus the new money invested, which is the same as the round's price per share multiplied by all fully diluted shares after the round. It is used to work out ownership: a new investor's stake equals the amount invested divided by the post-money valuation. Headline startup valuations, including unicorn status, usually refer to the post-money figure from the latest round. That price is paid for preference shares with special rights, so it can overstate what ordinary shares are worth. A common confusion: post-money valuation is not cash in the bank or a market price. It is a figure implied by one negotiated deal, and later rounds, an IPO or investor markdowns can put the company at a very different value.
example: Say XYZ AI raises $25 million at a $100 million pre-money valuation. Its post-money valuation is $125 million, and the new investors own $25 million / $125 million = 20%.
formula: Post-money valuation = Pre-money valuation + New investment; Investor ownership = New investment / Post-money valuation

short: The fall in an existing owner's percentage of a company when new shares are issued to someone else.
kid: You and a friend each own half of a lemonade stand. When a new friend joins and brings more lemons, everyone owns a smaller part, but the stand itself gets bigger.
detail: Equity dilution happens when a company issues new shares, which reduces the percentage ownership of existing shareholders. Common causes are new funding rounds, conversion of convertible notes or SAFEs, exercised employee stock options, warrants and acquisitions paid for in shares. A smaller percentage is not automatically a loss of value: if new money comes in at a higher valuation, a smaller slice of a bigger company can be worth more than before. Dilution hurts when shares are issued cheaply, as in a down round, or when the new cash does not create enough value. It also weakens control, since voting power falls with ownership. Founders track it through the cap table and fully diluted share count, and listed companies show it through diluted EPS. A common confusion: anti-dilution clauses do not prevent normal percentage dilution; they mainly protect investors when a later round is priced lower.
example: Say a founder owns 60 lakh of a company's 1 crore shares, or 60%. The company issues 25 lakh new shares to investors, taking the total to 1.25 crore, so the founder's stake falls to 60 lakh / 1.25 crore = 48%. If the round prices each share at ₹200, the founder's 60 lakh shares are worth ₹120 crore.
formula: Ownership after issue = Shares held / (Existing shares + New shares issued)

short: A table showing who owns a company's shares and share options, how much each owner holds, and how that changes after each funding round.
kid: It is a list on the fridge that shows how many slices of the family pizza each person has. When someone new gets a slice, the list is updated.
detail: A capitalisation table, or cap table, records every holder of a company's equity, such as founders, employees, angels and funds, broken down by type: ordinary shares, each series of preference shares, the ESOP pool, warrants, convertible notes and SAFEs. It shows shares held, percentage ownership on a basic and a fully diluted basis, and often the price paid. Founders and investors model the cap table before every round to see how new money, option pool top-ups and conversions will change ownership, and a waterfall analysis built on it shows who receives what in a sale once liquidation preferences are paid. In India, the cap table must match statutory records such as the register of members kept under the Companies Act, 2013. A common confusion: a neat percentage table can hide preferences and conversion terms, so the same ownership share can mean very different payouts.
example: Say before a seed round the founders hold 90 lakh shares and the ESOP pool 10 lakh, 1 crore in total. Seed investors buy 25 lakh new shares, so out of 1.25 crore fully diluted shares the founders hold 72%, the ESOP pool 8% and the seed investors 20%.
formula: Fully diluted ownership = Holder's shares and options / Total fully diluted shares

short: A rule letting certain investors take back their money first, before founders and staff get anything, when a company is sold or shut down.
kid: If the lemonade stand closes and only a few coins are left, the friend who gave coins at the start gets theirs back first. Everyone else shares what is left.
detail: A liquidation preference is a right attached to preference shares that sets the order and amount investors receive in a liquidation event, which in venture contracts usually includes a sale or merger of the company, not only a shutdown. A 1x preference entitles the investor to its original investment back before ordinary shareholders, such as founders and employees, are paid. With non-participating preferred, the investor chooses either its preference amount or converting to ordinary shares and taking its percentage share, whichever is larger. With participating preferred, it takes the preference and then also shares in what remains, often called a double dip. Multiples above 1x, and seniority between share series, tilt the payout further towards investors. A common confusion: a headline sale price says little about founder payouts; when a company sells for less than the total money raised, preferences can leave ordinary shareholders with little or nothing.
example: Say an investor put ₹30 crore into ABC Ltd for 25% with a 1x non-participating preference, and the company is sold for ₹80 crore. Converting would give 25% of ₹80 crore = ₹20 crore, so the investor takes its ₹30 crore preference instead and the other shareholders share the remaining ₹50 crore. With participating preferred, it would take ₹30 crore plus 25% of the remaining ₹50 crore, or ₹42.5 crore in total.
formula: Non-participating payout = max(Preference amount, Ownership % x Exit proceeds); Participating payout = Preference amount + Ownership % x (Exit proceeds - Preference amount)

short: A clause that gives earlier investors extra shares if the company later sells shares at a lower price than they paid.
kid: You swapped three sweets for a toy, and then your friend gets the same toy for just one sweet. To be fair, you are given an extra toy so your swap is not so bad.
detail: An anti-dilution provision protects holders of preference shares in a down round, when the company issues new shares below the price those investors paid. It works by lowering their conversion price, so each preference share converts into more ordinary shares. Under a full ratchet, the old conversion price drops all the way to the new, lower price, however few shares are issued, which is very harsh on founders. Under the far more common broad-based weighted average method, the adjustment depends on both how much lower the new price is and how many new shares are issued compared with the shares already outstanding. Routine issues such as ESOP grants are usually carved out. A common confusion: anti-dilution does not protect against ordinary percentage dilution in rounds priced higher; it applies only when shares are sold more cheaply, and the extra shares come at the expense of founders and other unprotected holders.
example: Say Series A investors paid ₹100 per share, and the company later issues Series B shares at ₹50. Under a full ratchet, the Series A conversion price drops to ₹50, so a ₹10 crore investment that bought 10 lakh preference shares now converts into 20 lakh ordinary shares.
formula: Weighted average: New conversion price = Old conversion price x (A + B) / (A + C), where A = shares outstanding before the issue, B = shares the new money would buy at the old price, C = new shares actually issued

short: A right letting majority shareholders force minority holders to join a sale of the company on the same terms, so a buyer gets full ownership.
kid: If most of the friends who share a toy box agree to give it to a new kid, the last friend has to go along too. That way the new kid gets the whole box.
detail: Drag-along rights, set out in a shareholders' agreement and usually the company's articles of association, let holders of an agreed majority, often including a particular class such as the preferred investors, require all other shareholders to sell when an approved buyer bids for the whole company. Dragged holders must accept the same price per share and terms, and typically must vote for and sign the deal. Buyers, especially in private equity buyouts, often want 100% ownership, so without this right a few holdouts could block a sale. Founders usually negotiate safeguards: a minimum price, a waiting period before it can be used, limits on the promises they must give the buyer, and approval thresholds that need both investor and founder votes. A common confusion: drag-along is the mirror image of tag-along; drag-along lets the majority force others to sell, while tag-along lets the minority choose to join a sale.
example: Say investors holding 75% of XYZ Software agree to sell the company for ₹400 per share, and the drag-along threshold is 70%. A founder holding 5 lakh shares who objects can be required to sell at the same price, receiving ₹20 crore.

short: A right letting minority shareholders join in when a major shareholder sells, at the same price and terms, so they are not left behind.
kid: If your big brother sells his half of the toy box to a new kid for sweets, you can say, 'Take mine too, for the same sweets.' Then you are not left behind.
detail: Tag-along rights, also called co-sale rights, protect minority shareholders when a controlling or major shareholder, often a founder or promoter, agrees to sell shares to an outside buyer. The minority holder can require the buyer to purchase a proportionate part of its shares, or in some deals all of them, at the same price and on the same terms. This stops a founder or majority owner from cashing out at a premium, perhaps handing control to an unknown buyer, while smaller investors stay locked in. In venture deals, investors usually hold tag-along rights over founder share sales, and in Indian private equity deals with promoter-run companies they are a standard investor protection in the shareholders' agreement. A common confusion: tag-along is optional for the minority, who may choose to sell, whereas drag-along is compulsory for the minority once the majority triggers it.
example: Say a founder owning 60% of ABC Ltd agrees to sell 30% of the company to a buyer, and an investor owns 20%. With a pro rata tag-along, the 30% being bought is shared between them in proportion to their holdings: the founder sells 30% x 60/80 = 22.5% and the investor 30% x 20/80 = 7.5%, both at the same price per share.

short: A right letting an existing shareholder or the company match an outside buyer's offer and buy the shares before that buyer can.
kid: If your friend wants to sell her bike to someone else, you get the first chance to buy it for the same price. Only if you say no can she sell it to them.
detail: A right of first refusal (ROFR) gives the company, its investors or both the right to buy shares that another shareholder, often a founder, wants to sell to an outsider, at the same price and terms the outsider has offered. The seller must first find a genuine buyer, then give holders notice and time to match. This keeps unwanted parties off the cap table and lets insiders increase their stake. A right of first offer (ROFO) works earlier in the process: the seller must first offer the shares to the rights holders, who can name a price, and only if they decline may the seller approach outsiders, usually at no lower price. Both are common in Indian shareholders' agreements. A common confusion: a ROFR lets the holder match a third party's offer, while a ROFO only gives the holder the first chance to make an offer.
example: Say a founder receives an outside offer of ₹300 per share for 1 lakh shares, ₹3 crore in total. The lead investor holds a ROFR, so it can buy those 1 lakh shares itself for ₹3 crore; if it declines within the notice period, the founder may sell to the outsider at no less than ₹300 per share.

short: A scheme that gives employees the right to buy company shares later at a fixed, usually low, price, rewarding them if the company grows.
kid: The owner of a lemonade stand tells a helper: stay and help, and later you can buy a piece of the stand for just a few coins. If the stand grows big, that piece becomes worth a lot.
detail: An employee stock option plan (ESOP) grants employees options: the right, but not the obligation, to buy a set number of shares at a fixed exercise price once the options vest. If the shares rise above that price, the employee gains the difference. Startups use ESOPs to attract and keep talent while paying less cash, and investors usually require an option pool, often 10% to 15% of fully diluted shares, to be set aside before a round. In India, ESOPs are governed by the Companies Act, 2013 and, for listed companies, by SEBI's share-based employee benefits regulations. Under tax rules as of 2025, the gain at exercise is generally taxed as a salary perquisite and any later gain on sale as capital gains, with deferral for eligible startups' employees. A common confusion: in the US, 'ESOP' usually means an employee stock ownership plan, a retirement trust that works differently.
example: Say an employee at XYZ Fintech is granted 4,000 options with an exercise price of ₹50. After they vest, the shares are valued at ₹550 each, so exercising costs ₹2 lakh and gives shares worth ₹22 lakh, a pre-tax gain of ₹20 lakh.
formula: Option gain = (Share value - Exercise price) x Number of options exercised

short: The timetable over which an employee or founder gradually earns full ownership of the shares or options they were granted, by staying with the company.
kid: Grandma says you will get one new toy for every month you help in the garden. You only keep the toys for the months you have already helped.
detail: A vesting schedule sets when granted shares or options become the holder's to keep. A typical startup schedule runs four years with a one-year cliff: nothing vests in the first year, 25% vests on the first anniversary, and the rest vests monthly or quarterly over the next three years. If the person leaves early, unvested options go back into the pool. Founders often accept reverse vesting on their own shares, letting the company buy back unvested shares if a founder quits. Acceleration clauses can speed up vesting when the company is sold: single-trigger on the sale alone, double-trigger on a sale followed by the person losing their job. In India, under the rules as of 2025, the minimum gap between grant and vesting is one year. A common confusion: vested options still have to be exercised, by paying the exercise price, before the holder owns shares.
example: Say an employee is granted 4,800 options vesting over four years with a one-year cliff. Nothing vests for 12 months, then 1,200 options vest at once and 100 more vest each month for the next 36 months. If she leaves after 30 months, she has 1,200 + 18 x 100 = 3,000 vested options.
formula: Vested options (after the cliff) = Total grant x Months of service / Total vesting months

short: A loan to a startup that usually turns into shares at its next funding round, often at a discount, instead of being repaid in cash.
kid: A friend lends your lemonade stand some coins. Later, instead of giving the coins back, you give your friend a piece of the stand, and a slightly bigger piece as a thank-you for helping early.
detail: A convertible note is a loan from an early investor to a startup that is expected to convert into shares at a future priced round rather than be repaid. It carries interest, which usually accrues and converts too, and a maturity date. To reward early risk, notes often include a discount to the next round's price, a valuation cap that sets the highest valuation used for conversion, or both, with the investor getting whichever gives the lower price. Notes let both sides postpone agreeing a valuation and close quickly. If no round happens by maturity, the note may be repaid, extended or converted on agreed terms. In India, under the rules as of 2025, convertible notes are mainly limited to DPIIT-recognised startups raising at least ₹25 lakh per tranche. A common confusion: a SAFE looks similar but is not debt, so it has no interest or maturity.
example: Say an angel lends ₹50 lakh to ABC Ltd through a convertible note with a 20% discount. At the next round new investors pay ₹250 per share, so the note converts at ₹200 per share and the angel receives 25,000 shares, ignoring interest.
formula: Conversion price = lower of [Next round price x (1 - Discount)] and [Valuation cap / Fully diluted shares before the round]; Shares received = (Principal + Accrued interest) / Conversion price

short: A contract where an investor gives a startup money now for shares later, when the company next raises money at an agreed value.
kid: A friend gives you coins now, and you promise them a piece of your lemonade stand later, once everyone agrees how much the stand is worth.
detail: A SAFE (simple agreement for future equity) was introduced by Y Combinator in 2013 as a lighter alternative to the convertible note. The investor pays now and gets the right to shares at a future priced round, usually at a price set by a valuation cap, a discount, or both. Unlike a note, a SAFE is not debt: it has no interest and no maturity date. If the company is sold before a priced round, the holder typically gets the greater of its money back or what it would receive on conversion; if the company fails, it may get nothing. Since 2018 the standard US form is the post-money SAFE, which fixes the holder's ownership percentage before the next round's money. In India, SAFE-style deals are usually adapted, often as compulsorily convertible preference shares, to fit Indian law. A common confusion: 'SAFE' does not mean low risk.
example: Say an investor puts $500,000 into a startup through a post-money SAFE with a $10 million valuation cap. At the next priced round the SAFE converts into $500,000 / $10 million = 5% of the company as measured just before the new money, and that 5% is then diluted by the new round.
formula: Post-money SAFE ownership (before the new round) = Investment amount / Post-money valuation cap

short: The highest company value used to turn an early investor's money into shares later, so they get a fair price if the company grows fast.
kid: A friend gives you coins today and you promise them toys later. You also promise that, however popular your toys become, they will never have to pay more than a set price.
detail: A valuation cap is a term in convertible notes and SAFEs that sets the maximum valuation at which the investment converts into shares. If the next priced round values the company above the cap, the early investor converts as if the valuation were only the cap, getting more shares per rupee or dollar than the new investors. If the round is priced below the cap, the cap does not bite and the investor converts at the round price, less any discount. The cap rewards early investors for taking risk before any valuation was set. Caps can be pre-money or post-money, which changes who bears dilution: a post-money cap fixes the investor's percentage, so each extra SAFE dilutes only the existing holders, mainly the founders. A common confusion: the cap is not the company's valuation. It is only a ceiling on the conversion price.
example: Say an investor holds a ₹1 crore SAFE with a ₹10 crore pre-money cap, and the company later raises at ₹40 crore pre-money with 40 lakh shares, or ₹100 per share. The cap price is ₹10 crore / 40 lakh = ₹25 per share, so the SAFE converts into ₹1 crore / ₹25 = 4 lakh shares instead of the 1 lakh shares the round price would give.
formula: Cap price per share = Valuation cap / Fully diluted shares before conversion; Conversion price = lower of Cap price and Round price (after any discount)

short: Loans made to startups that already have venture capital backing, letting them raise extra cash without selling as many shares.
kid: A lemonade stand that already has helpers borrows some extra coins and promises to pay them back over time. That way it does not have to give away more pieces of the stand.
detail: Venture debt is a loan, usually lasting two to four years, to startups that have raised venture capital but may lack profits or assets to pledge. Lenders rely on the strength of the equity investors behind the company and its ability to raise again, so loans are often sized as a fraction of the last equity round. Besides interest and fees, lenders often take warrants, small rights to buy shares, for extra return. Startups use venture debt to extend runway, fund working capital or equipment, or reach the next milestone with less dilution. In India, specialist funds, some banks and NBFCs provide it, often as debentures. A common confusion: venture debt is cheaper than equity only if things go well. It must be repaid on schedule and usually comes with covenants, so it becomes risky when growth slows and the next round is delayed.
example: Say a startup valued at ₹500 crore pre-money needs ₹50 crore. Raising it as equity would mean selling ₹50 crore / ₹550 crore, about 9.1% of the company, while venture debt at 14% a year costs ₹7 crore of interest in the first year plus a small warrant stake, and the ₹50 crore must be repaid.

short: How fast a company spends its cash, usually measured per month, when its spending is larger than the money coming in.
kid: If you spend five coins from your piggy bank every week and nobody adds any, your coins slowly disappear. How fast they disappear is the burn.
detail: Burn rate measures how quickly a loss-making company uses up its cash. Gross burn is total monthly cash spending on salaries, rent, marketing, technology and other costs. Net burn is gross burn minus cash coming in from customers, and it is the figure investors focus on most. Burn rate together with cash in the bank sets the runway, the number of months before the money runs out. A high burn can be acceptable if it buys fast, efficient growth, and investors use measures such as the burn multiple (net burn divided by net new annual recurring revenue) to judge whether spending is productive. During the 2022-23 funding slowdown, many Indian and global startups cut burn through layoffs and lower marketing spend to stretch their runway. A common confusion: burn rate is about cash, not accounting profit; depreciation does not burn cash, while equipment purchases and advance payments do.
example: Say XYZ Edtech spends ₹6 crore a month and collects ₹2 crore a month from customers. Its gross burn is ₹6 crore, its net burn is ₹4 crore, and with ₹48 crore in the bank its runway is ₹48 crore / ₹4 crore = 12 months.
formula: Net burn rate = Cash spent in the period - Cash received in the period (usually per month)

short: The number of months a company can keep operating with the cash it has, if its spending and income stay at the current pace.
kid: If your piggy bank has twenty coins and you spend five each week, you can keep buying treats for four weeks. Those four weeks are your runway.
detail: Runway is how long a company can survive before it runs out of cash, assuming no new funding and no change in its burn rate. It is calculated by dividing current cash and easily sold investments by monthly net burn. Founders and investors watch it closely because raising a new round usually takes several months, so fundraising must start well before cash runs low; a common rule of thumb is to have 18 to 24 months of runway after a raise. A short runway weakens a company's bargaining power and can force a bridge round, a down round, layoffs or a sale on poor terms. Runway can be lengthened by cutting costs, growing revenue, raising equity or taking venture debt. A common confusion: the simple calculation assumes burn stays flat, but burn usually rises with hiring and growth, so the real runway is often shorter than the headline number.
example: Say ABC Mobility has ₹60 crore in cash and a net burn of ₹5 crore a month, giving 12 months of runway. If it cuts net burn to ₹4 crore a month, its runway stretches to 15 months.
formula: Runway (months) = Cash and liquid investments / Monthly net burn

short: A privately owned startup valued at $1 billion or more, usually based on its latest funding round, before it lists on a stock exchange.
kid: A unicorn is a magical animal that is very hard to find. A tiny new business that grows super, super big is just as rare, so people call it a unicorn.
detail: A unicorn is a privately held startup valued at $1 billion or more. Investor Aileen Lee coined the term in 2013 to stress how rare such companies were. Bigger labels followed: a decacorn is valued at $10 billion or more and a hectocorn at $100 billion or more, while 'soonicorn', popular in India, describes startups expected to reach unicorn status soon. The valuation usually comes from the post-money price of the latest funding round, which is paid for preference shares with special rights, so it can overstate what the whole company would fetch in a sale or IPO. India has become one of the world's largest unicorn ecosystems, with a record number of new Indian unicorns created in the 2021 funding boom. A common confusion: unicorn status does not mean profit or lasting success; many unicorns make losses, and some have lost the tag after down rounds or investor markdowns.
example: Say XYZ Logistics raises $100 million at a $900 million pre-money valuation. Its post-money valuation is $1 billion, which makes it a unicorn on paper, even if it still reports losses.

short: A funding round in which a startup sells new shares at a lower price, and so a lower valuation, than in its previous round.
kid: Last summer people paid three sweets for a cup of your lemonade. This summer they will only pay two. Getting less than before is what this means.
detail: A down round happens when a private company raises money at a price per share below the price in its previous round, usually because growth disappointed, burn was too high or markets turned, as in the 2022-23 tech funding slowdown. It hurts existing holders in several ways: dilution is larger, anti-dilution clauses can hand earlier investors extra shares at founders' expense, employee options can go underwater, with the exercise price above the share value, and morale and reputation can suffer. New investors often demand tougher terms, such as stronger liquidation preferences. A flat round, at the same price as before, avoids a cut but often signals stalled growth. A common confusion: a down round is an actual sale of new shares at a lower price, while a valuation markdown is an investor lowering the value of its holding in its own books without any new shares being sold.
example: Say ABC Ltd raised its Series B at ₹500 per share, valuing it at ₹1,000 crore post-money with 2 crore shares. It now raises ₹150 crore at ₹300 per share, a 40% lower price and a pre-money valuation of ₹600 crore, so the new investors get 50 lakh shares, or 20% of the company, before any anti-dilution adjustment.

short: A cut by an investor in the value it reports for its stake in a private company, without any shares actually being bought or sold.
kid: You thought your toy car could be swapped for ten sweets, but now you think it would only get six. You write the smaller number in your notebook, even though you have not swapped it.
detail: A valuation markdown occurs when an investor lowers the fair value at which it carries a holding in its own books. Venture capital funds, mutual funds and other holders of unlisted shares must value their investments regularly, using recent deal prices, multiples of comparable listed companies and discounted cash flows. When listed peers fall, growth slows or governance problems emerge, they mark the holding down; raising it again is a markup. Some large global mutual funds disclose these values in regular filings, so markdowns of well-known Indian startups often make news. A markdown changes the investor's reported returns, such as net asset value or interim IRR, but the company itself raises no money and issues no shares. A common confusion: a markdown is one investor's estimate, not a transaction; a down round is an actual sale of new shares at a lower price, though repeated markdowns often hint at one.
example: Say a fund holds 1% of XYZ Tech, bought when the company was valued at $5 billion, so the stake was carried at $50 million. After listed peers fall, the fund values the company at $3 billion, so the stake is now carried at $30 million, a 40% markdown, even though no shares were sold.
formula: Markdown % = (Previous carrying value - New carrying value) / Previous carrying value
